newsitem.title: MOLDOVA: Russia's GAZ 1996 profit likely to halve.
newsitem.headline: Russia's GAZ 1996 profit likely to halve.

text.p: Russian carmaker GAZ expects its net profit to halve this year to 650-700 billion roubles because of a big increase in taxes, its chief executive said on Friday.

"The sharp fall in profits expected this year has nothing to do with our efficiency," GAZ chief executive Nikolai Pugin told Reuters after cutting a ribbon to open a joint venture in Moldova GAZelle mini-trucks in the capital Chisinau.
Last year AO Gorkovsky Avtomobilny Zavod netted 1.4 trillion roubles on sales of over eight trillion.
"But in line with a government decision, the value of GAZ's fixed assets was increased three-fold in January this year, and now the company has to pay much higher taxes on its property," Pugin said.
The figures are to Russian accounting standards, which are designed to meet the needs of the tax authorities rather than to give a picture of the health or profitability of a company.
In the first nine months of this year GAZ netted 330 billion roubles, less than in the same period last year, Pugin said.

Profits could fall further next year, as the government was planning a new re-evaluation in January. "We can do nothing about it -- GAZ is a profitable company, and the authorities want to keep loss-makers afloat at our expense," Pugin said.
The government, hit by a serious short-fall in revenues, is doing all it can to increase tax collection from corporations.
This week the powerful gas monopoly RAO Gazprom, Russia's biggest company, said some of its assets had been frozen by the authorities, who are trying to collect tax arrears.

"But despite all the difficulties we are still a fast growing company," Pugin said. According to his estimates, GAZ produced in the first nine months of this year some 155,000 cars and trucks, 8.8 percent above year-ago levels.

Pugin said he expected GAZ this year to exceed its 1995 production figure of 200,000 cars and trucks. Last year GAZ accounted for 14 percent of Russia's automotive output, compared to seven percent in 1989, a company press release said.

"We have decreased the output trucks for the army and agriculture, for which they do not pay. But we hope to boost the output of Volga saloons and GAZelle trucks by five and 18 percent, respectively, this year," he said.
GAZ also hopes to produce this year 5,000 of its new 8- and 13-seat minibuses.
